![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Bradley Barcola, Bruno Fernandes, Julian Alvarez]() The summer window is kicking into another gear as the likes of Arsenal, Manchester United, Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham work on deals to improve their squads before the start of the new Premier League season. The Gunners continue to be linked with Julian Alvarez and Victor Osimhen to bolster their attack, while Ezri Konsa and Jarrel Quansah continue to be of interest in defence. Man United are aware of interest in Bruno Guimaraes, amid reports of a £43million bid from Galatasaray, and are said to be interested in Adam Wharton and Kim Min-jae. Meanwhile, Liverpool have agreed personal terms with Ibrahim Mbaye as they take another huge step towards a double deal including Paris Saint-Germain star Bradley Barcola. Chelsea are braced for a Man City bid for Enzo Fernandez following Rodri’s move to Barcelona, while Pedro Neto has admirers in Saudi Arabia. Tottenham are closing in on the signing of Savinho and hope to then add Cody Gakpo to their forward line. Follow the latest transfer news, rumours and gossip live below! Latest transfer news and rumours Live updates Newcastle still keen on £50m Lucas Bergvall Newcastle United remain interested in signing Tottenham midfielder Lucas Bergvall. According to the Daily Mail, Matthias Jaissle’s side are considering Bergvall as a potential replacement for former captain Bruno Guimaraes. The 20-year-old is regarded as one of Europe’s most promising young midfielders, but earlier this summer asked to leave after not being guaranteed regular first-team football. Tottenham are understood to value Bergvall at around £50m. Liverpool to submit new Bradley Barcola bid Liverpool are set to submit a fresh bid for Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola as they close in on a deal for Ibrahim Mbaye. According to RMC Sport, a deal to sign Mbaye is progressing quickly after the player reached an agreement with Liverpool over a five-year contract. Liverpool are also deep in talks over Barcola, with a new bid expected this week. PSG want a potential club-record fee for the France star. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/01KZRTW82CCT9NK9YH60MGADZ1.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Atletico send Alvarez transfer message to Arsenal after 'Arteta talks' Julian Alvarez has been left out of Atletico Madrid's first La Liga game of the season, but the striker remains not for sale amid interest from Barcelona and Arsenal. The Argentine has been Barcelona's top transfer target all summer, with the player having repeatedly voiced his desire to move to the Camp Nou. Arsenal have long been interested in the former Manchester City forward, with Mikel Arteta reportedly driving the club's interest, but it is Barca were Alvarez wishes to go. Atletico have other ideas, and have repeated privately and publicly ruled out a summer exit for the striker. “It’s like when you go to court, that’s it, there’s nothing more to it. We’re looking after both the person and the player, and we understand that he is not in the right condition to play in this match." ![Julian Alvarez](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/11/44/alvarez.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Tottenham set Richarlison transfer stance Tottenham will demand a sizeable fee if they are to sell Richarlison before the close of the summer transfer window, writes Sam Tabuteau. There had been concerns that Spurs could lose the Brazilian striker, who is attracting interest from Everton, on the cheap with a year remaining on his current contract. But Standard Sport understands that Spurs retain the option to extend Richarlison’s contract by an extra 12 months, meaning they will not be forced into a cut-price sale. Spurs signed Richarlison from Everton in a deal worth around £60million in 2022. Richarlison finished last season as Spurs’ top goalscorer in all competitions, netting 11 times in the Premier League as the north London club narrowly avoided relegation. Despite playing a pivotal role in Spurs keeping their Premier League status, the 29-year-old continues to be linked with a move away. A return to his homeland, or former club Everton, have been mooted. ![

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/15/14/01M02V3KG7EVNXGMVVCAD3Z7V6.jpg?trim=0,0,226,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Man United, Newcastle and Tottenham monitor Edmond Tapsoba Manchester United, Newcastle United and Tottenham are monitoring Bayer Leverkusen defender Edmond Tapsoba. According to Fussballdaten, Leverkusen would be willing to discuss a deal for the 27-year-old centre-back at around €50m (£42.7m), despite his contract running until 2031. Tapsoba has been an important player for Leverkusen since joining from Vitória Guimarães in 2020 and has made more than 270 competitive appearances for the Bundesliga club. All three Premier League clubs are reportedly in contact with the Burkina Faso international’s representatives as they assess the possibility of a summer move. Chelsea demand £100m for Pedro Neto Chelsea are demanding a fee of £100m for Pedro Neto, Dom Smith reports. The Portuguese winger is attracting interest from Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal, having also been linked with the likes of Manchester City, Tottenham and Liverpool this summer. However, Chelsea are not actively looking to sell Neto and would ask for an eye-watering £100m to entertain any prospect of a sale. Chelsea’s high valuation of Neto has been influenced by the inflated winger market elsewhere in Europe. Man Utd being new contract talks with Bruno Fernandes Manchester United have opened contract talks with Bruno Fernandes and insist he is not for sale at any price amid interest from Turkish giants Galatasaray, writes Sam Tabuteau. Standard Sport understands that United are determined to keep hold of their influential captain this summer and have held preliminary talks over a new deal. Fernandes’ current contract at Old Trafford expires next summer, but United, who have the option to extend it by a further 12 months, are relaxed about the situation and already in the process of negotiating fresh terms The Portuguese international enjoyed a stellar campaign last season as United qualified for the Champions League, breaking the single season assist record in the Premier League. Fernandes is viewed as a critical part of manager Michael Carrick’s plans. However, interest has begun to build in his services with clubs aware that he could leave on a free transfer next summer There was previously a £57million release clause in Fernandes’ contract, but that expired this summer and United have now made their stance on the former Sporting midfielder clear. ![

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/17/20/01M087ESDKKD461P1X06HMC9VS.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Official! Newcastle sign Amar Dedic Newcastle have signed defender Amar Dedic from Benfica in a deal worth around £30m. Dedic has signed a five-year deal to reunite with manager Matthias Jaissle, with whom he previously won the Austrian title at Red Bull Salzburg in 2023. "It's a special feeling and a really big honour for me to join Newcastle United," he said after the move was announced on Tuesday, his 24th birthday. "I'm really happy to be here and can't wait to start playing for the club and the amazing fans. "Working with Matthias again was a big factor for me. We know each other well. He knows what I can bring on the pitch and I'm really happy to be playing for him again. "Playing Premier League football at St James' Park is going to be really special. Every game feels like a big occasion, with an amazing atmosphere. I'm really excited to get started." Arsenal monitor Marc Pubill and attacking targets Arsenal remain keen to strengthen their defence and attack during the final days of the window. The Gunners made enquiries about Atletico Madrid defender Marc Pubill before the summer transfer window, but the Spanish club are equally determined to keep the 23-year-old. The Athletic report that left wing is Arsenal’s priority, though could move for a right-sided forward if the right opportunity becomes available. Kenan Yildiz and Julian Alvarez remain long-term targets, with Arsenal waiting to see if either becomes available before deciding whether to pursue alternative options. Manchester United open Bruno Fernandes contract talks Manchester United are in contract talks with Bruno Fernandes after the midfielder received a lucrative proposal from Galatasaray. According to The Athletic, the Turkish club offered the 31-year-old a salary of €20m (£17.1m) per year, but Fernandes wants to remain at United and is discussing a new deal. His current contract runs until 2027, with an option for a further year. A €65m release clause available to foreign clubs has also now expired. United are not open to selling Fernandes and maintain they have received no contact from other clubs over the Portugal international.
8750e52fb8b70a273de6e11d.summary: Premier League clubs are actively working on summer transfer deals and squad improvements as the window progresses. Key developments include Liverpool nearing a double deal involving Ibrahim Mbaye and Bradley Barcola, Manchester United opening contract talks with Bruno Fernandes, and Newcastle United completing the signing of Amar Dedic from Benfica for £30 million. Meanwhile, clubs like Arsenal, Chelsea, and Tottenham face high valuations or resistance from parent clubs regarding targets such as Julian Alvarez and Pedro Neto.
key_points: Newcastle United signed defender Amar Dedic from Benfica on a five-year deal for approximately £30 million.
Liverpool have agreed personal terms with Ibrahim Mbaye and are preparing a fresh bid for PSG winger Bradley Barcola.
Manchester United have opened contract talks with Bruno Fernandes and insist he is not for sale amid interest from Galatasaray.
Atletico Madrid have ruled out a summer exit for Julian Alvarez despite strong interest from Arsenal and Barcelona.
Chelsea have placed a £100 million valuation on Pedro Neto amid interest from Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal.

820c33af2f9294ab00983655.title: Bizarre 'jellyfish spotted on Mars' in resurfaced Nasa images
820c33af2f9294ab00983655.author: Josh Milton
820c33af2f9294ab00983655.content:
![Side-by-side images show a tripod- shaped object on Mars.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/picture-nasa.png?w=646) 
When we think of Martians, we tend to think of little grey men.
But if a resurfaced image taken by a Nasa rover is anything to go by, the aliens that call Mars home are land-walking ‘jellyfish’. Maybe.
The photo was taken by Curiosity in August 2023, 3,924 Martian days, or Sols, into the extraterrestrial explorer’s time exploring the red planet.
The black-and-white panorama shows the 96-mile-wide Gale Crater, an ancient meteor impact crater, with a black, spindly object on the slopes.
Curiosity, a 1,000kg mobile laboratory sent to analyse Martian soil and rocks, frequently took photographs as it trundled around.
Strangely, the dark object was not there in a photograph taken less than 10 seconds before. It was also the final photo taken that day.
The image caption provides no further information beyond saying the shot was taken by the Right Navigation Camera.
Kari Sivertzen, who has for months been rummaging through images taken by Curiosity, flagged the image on the social media platform X last week.
Users weren’t entirely sure what to make of the object, with Sivertzen insisting it wasn’t Ingenuity, a tiny helicopter that stands on spindly legs.
Ingenuity acted as a scout for the life-seeking probe, Perseverance, which was about 2,300 miles away in the Jezero Crater.
Could it be a UFO?
Jean Ward, a Mars researcher, said the ‘tripod object’ could be a ‘potential UFO’, or Unidentified Flying Object.
‘As always, until we get boots on the ground to see these anomalies up close, I can only speculate as to what these objects might be,’ he said.
Another user added: ‘What on Mars is that?!’
While a third user commented: ‘First image of a jellyfish UFO [on] Mars. Great.’
After all, many, many things have been spotted on Mars that, at first glance, shouldn’t be there. From egg-shaped holes and ‘spiders‘ to rolling hills that resemble the ruins of a city and a ‘crowned face’.
But sceptics said that, like those examples above, this tripod-shaped object could simply be a trick of the light or something our human brains are trying to make sense of too creatively.
![NASA image showing 'doorway' on Mars](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_303745495-92ba.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
![NASA?s Curiosity Mars rover took this selfie at a location nicknamed ?Mary Anning? after a 19th-century English palaeontologist in this image released by the U.S. space agency on Nov 12, 2020. Curiosity snagged three samples of drilled rock at this site on its way out of the Glen Torridon region, which scientists believe preserves an ancient habitable environment. NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY.](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_294017766-0e4b.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Some questioned whether the object was what space officials call an ‘artefact’. Rather than a lost relic, this term refers to smudge-shaped corrupted pixels and other glitches in cameras when taking a photo.
Nasa has been approached for comment.
Sivertzen said in June that he’s digging through the Martian probe archives so he can share anything that ‘captures his eye’.
‘I believe there is life on other planets, and since NASA has found potential traces of life on Mars, it’s the perfect place to look.’
Curiosity hoped the same. The craft has been roaming Gale Crater since 2012, looking for tiny traces of life etched in centuries-old rocks.
What do you think the 'jellyfish' on Mars is?
- 
						It's an extraterrestrial anomaly.
- 
						It's just a photographic glitch.
- 
						It could be something explainable, but mysterious.
- 
						I'm not sure what to believe.
‘Jellyfish’ from another world have visited the Earth before – kind of.
- 
	![Five youths killed in wrong-way motorway crash](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308672600-f287.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- Five boys killed in wrong way motorway crash ‘were in car linked to burglary gang’
- Major rail operator serving London issues urgent 'do not travel' warning
- Trump threatens to 'bomb the s***' out of' another country
On February 10, 1989, people in Wiltshire and Gloucestershire craned their necks up high to see a UFO shaped like the gelatinous creature.
Witnesses, who included police officers, said the object was ‘larger than a helicopter with more lights than a plane’.
Similar dangly objects, now known as Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP), have been seen floating above military bases in Iraq.
But sceptics say such objects could easily be a bedraggled balloon or an aircraft.
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.
For more stories like this, check our news page.
820c33af2f9294ab00983655.summary: Resurfaced NASA images taken by the Curiosity rover in August 2023 show a strange, tripod-shaped, black object on the slopes of Mars' Gale Crater. While some social media users and a Mars researcher speculated the anomaly could be a UFO or a 'jellyfish' alien, sceptics suggested it may be a trick of the light or a photographic camera glitch known as an artefact. The Curiosity rover, which landed in 2012 to analyze Martian soil and rocks, provided no further information in the image caption.
key_points: The photo was captured by NASA's Curiosity rover in August 2023 at the Gale Crater on Mars.
The black, spindly object appeared in the final photo of the day and was absent in a picture taken less than 10 seconds prior.
Mars researcher Jean Ward suggested the tripod-shaped anomaly could be a potential UFO.
Sceptics believe the object is likely a trick of the light, a creative human interpretation, or a camera glitch artefact.

The black, spindly object appeared in the final photo of the day and was absent in a picture taken less than 10 seconds prior.

Sceptics believe the object is likely a trick of the light, a creative human interpretation, or a camera glitch artefact.

524c2229c2393d702d62bf53.title: Andy Burnham says he's not embarrassed about hoax message exchange
524c2229c2393d702d62bf53.author: Richard Wheeler
524c2229c2393d702d62bf53.content:
PM Andy Burnham says there was "a minimal exchange of information of zero consequence"
- Published
Andy Burnham says he is not embarrassed that he exchanged messages with a person posing as US President Donald Trump's chief of staff.
The prime minister added all politicians face "these challenges" but insisted he did "everything right" in how he handled the security breach.
News website Politico first reported, external that Burnham communicated with a person claiming to be Susie Wiles. Burnham said there was a "minimal exchange of information of zero consequence".
Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary has written to Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) to ask them to consider investigating what he called an "egregious security breach".
It is understood the communication between Burnham and the person posing as Wiles was in the form of messages and there was no conversation between the two.
Asked if he was embarrassed about the incident, Burnham told broadcasters: "No, I am not because there was a minimal exchange, nothing of consequence and quickly I realised that this needed to be reported and I did so.
"So I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right."
Pressed on what action is being taken to find out who was behind the incident and to improve systems, Burnham said the "correct action" had been taken both in the UK and the US, without providing further details.
MacCleary, in his letter to ISC chairman Lord Beamish, said the security of the prime minister's communications "ought to be an absolute priority".
He added: "We need to understand how this breach could occur, or else risk it being repeated."
On Monday, Downing Street did not say when the messages were exchanged, or how many there were, nor whether they were over WhatsApp or another system.
A White House official told the BBC on Monday that the latest incident "had nothing to do" with Wiles' phone being hacked.
The BBC previously reported an FBI probe into Wiles' personal phone being hacked in May last year.
Wiles, a key Trump ally, told people at the time that her phone had been hacked after an impersonator - or impersonators - used her contacts file to message other top US officials.
Burnham is not the first high-profile UK political figure to have come into contact with an imposter.
In 2024, the Foreign Office confirmed then-foreign secretary Lord Cameron had been the victim of a hoax call in which someone pretended to be former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko.
Former Prime Minister Lord Cameron also exchanged some text messages with the impersonator pretending to be Poroshenko, who was president of Ukraine between 2014 and 2019.
The Foreign Office said it released details of the exchange publicly over fears it could be "manipulated".

39d084d50a096dab94c53104.title: State pension on course to rise by £500 next year
39d084d50a096dab94c53104.author: Rob White
39d084d50a096dab94c53104.content:
Retirees could receive a £500 boost to their state pension next year if wage growth continues to outpace inflation, figures suggest.
The new state pension is on course to rise by £515 to £13,062 and the basic state pension by £395 to £10,010 from next year, according to Hargreaves Lansdown.
The benefit is expected to increase at the same rate as wages for the fourth successive year, boosting pensioners’ payouts by around 4.1pc.
Both payments increase each year by the highest of wage growth, inflation or 2.5pc, thanks to the triple lock.
The annual state pension increase has been tied to wage growth for the past three years, resulting in boosts of up to 8.5pc.

c8c6da0a6dd8bbb6e8193dab.title: Watch European astronaut make history during spacewalk today
c8c6da0a6dd8bbb6e8193dab.author: Mike Wall
c8c6da0a6dd8bbb6e8193dab.content:
![LIVE FROM ISS: First French Woman to Spacewalk tasked with replacing Space-to-Ground Antenna - YouTube](https://img.youtube.com/vi/gXwLYq2ZsLM/maxresdefault.jpg) 
Sophie Adenot will make spaceflight history today (Aug. 18).
The European Space Agency (ESA) astronaut will become the first French woman ever to conduct a spacewalk, an activity she'll undertake with NASA astronaut Anil Menon.
The duo are scheduled to step outside the International Space Station (ISS) for a 6.5-hour excursion today at around 8:35 a.m. EDT (1235 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA. Coverage starts at 7 a.m. EDT (1100 GMT).
 ![a smiling woman in a white polo shirt sits in front of black drapes](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2zC5KQaMAC25gNRST9USCh.jpg) 
Adenot and Menon will "replace a space-to-ground antenna on the orbital complex," NASA officials wrote in a spacewalk preview.
"The antenna is a critical communications link NASA uses to transmit data, enabling high-speed communications between the Mission Control Center in Houston and the space station," they added.
This will be the second spacewalk for Menon; his first one, conducted with fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Meir, occurred on Aug. 6. During that extravehicular activity (EVA), a carbon dioxide sensor on Menon's spacesuit gave "an unexpected data reading," NASA officials wrote in an Aug. 7 update.
The sensor returned to normal after Menon doffed the suit, but NASA took some extra time to make sure there was no serious issue. As a result, the agency pushed his second spacewalk back a few days — from the originally planned Aug. 13 to today.
Today's spacewalk will be the 282nd overall in the long history of the ISS. Menon, who reached orbit on a Russian Soyuz spacecraft on July 14, will be "crewmember 1" on the EVA. Adenot — a member of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission, which reached the orbiting lab in February — will be "crewmember 2."
Adenot won't be the first French person overall to conduct an EVA. That distinction goes to Jean-Loup Chrétien, who performed a spacewalk outside the then-Soviet Union's Mir space station in 1988.
Other male French astronauts, including Philippe Perrin and Thomas Pesquet, later spacewalked outside the ISS. Pesquet also became the first French person to command an ISS mission, taking the reins in October 2021.

2c2695d5002a972bda7c2cd8.title: Cambridge University vice-chancellor heckled at Jason Arday vigil
2c2695d5002a972bda7c2cd8.author: Mousumi Bakshi; Elliot Deady
2c2695d5002a972bda7c2cd8.content:
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil in Cambridge city centre on Monday
- Published
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge was heckled as she was seen in public for the first time since the death of former professor Jason Arday.
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism in Cambridge city centre on Monday evening.
Shouting from a signpost in the city's market square, one attendee called Prentice "shameful" for failing to attend another event organised by Arday's students on Sunday.
Prentice previously said the university was "deeply saddened" by the academic's death.
![Dressed in a black turtle neck and trousers, Jason Arday smiles at the camera in a BBC Radio 4 studio.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/ea6e/live/9024e850-988b-11f1-83ef-33838a09c7c1.jpg)
Jason Arday was found dead in Battersea, south London, on Friday
Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
He resigned from his role at the university earlier this month after facing allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims and, in one case, had been cleared.
Asked about the heckling at the vigil, Cambridge University said: "The vice-chancellor attended the vigil to pay her respects.
"She understands that this is a very difficult time for many people. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason's family and loved ones, who have lost a father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
Concerns over media scrutiny
Arday's death sparked a debate over whether the media scrutiny was excessive or justified by his prominence.
Anger at the level of media coverage he had been subjected to was felt by many of the people who spoke to the BBC at the rally.
Addressing a crowd, Melanie Benedict, undergraduate president of Cambridge's students' union, said Arday had faced "disproportionate public scrutiny" which "would've been unbearable for anyone".
"The systemic issues that academics of colour have to face year on year have been highlighted by the tragedy of Jason's public treatment and subsequent death," they said.
![A woman - Milli Akehurst - looking at the camera with a neutral expression. She is wearing sunglasses and standing in front of a market, with a group of people behind her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3ad0/live/2faa4f50-9afd-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Milli Akehurst's son studies law at Cambridge
Reflecting on the press coverage, the National Education Union's Cambridgeshire secretary Abby Maddison said: "It doesn't feel right, what has been happening to him."
Milli Akehurst, whose son studies law at Cambridge, said: "It really saddens me the fact that as a black mother who has a son that comes hereâ¦ to see this happening is just heartbreaking.
"I think racism played a big part in [what happened to Arday]. He was cleared [of plagiarism], so why did it continue, and why were there so many articles within the last month or few weeks?"
![A crowd of people standing in a market square looking on as they are addressed by a speaker at a vigil.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/b95d/live/6a4c6c00-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Crowds gathered in Cambridge's market square as part of a vigil organised by Stand Up to Racism
Tachya Brobbey said she had been "very moved and very upset" that Arday had been "so trodden into the ground by the media".
"Clearly there was a disproportionate focus on him. We know there are others where there have been allegations that haven't had that amount of attention.
"Equally, I can see parallels with people like Caroline Flack where the media go for someone and destroy them. I think there are lots of layers to this but, yes, racism is a feature of it and it would be naive to think it wasn't."
![A woman - Shareena Howley - looking straight at the camera with a neutral expression. She is wearing a black sleeveless T-shirt and is standing in front of a row of shops and a takeaway food outlet.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/8deb/live/a044a520-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.jpg)
Shareena Howley held back tears as she spoke about Jason Arday
Shareena Howley, who had met Arday, said: "He was gentle, he was intelligent, maybe he did make some mistakes but did he really deserve that? Did he really deserve to be hounded to death?"
"He was about empowerment. He didn't shut the doors behind him, he said 'here's the ladder, I will pull you up'," she said, holding back tears.
The 54-year-old said there had been other Cambridge professors who had faced similar accusations: "Where was the press then?"
![A cardboard sign with the words "shame on the British media. Digital lynching" among floral tributes.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/e0ea/live/f96320f0-9afe-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Tributes were left in Trafalgar Square, central London, where another vigil was held on Monday
Plagiarism row
The plagiarism row began after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he had found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.
Cofnas's post had been terminated after a backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".
Cambridge had celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible minority in academia. Only 1% of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.
The university's chancellor Lord Smith criticised the "racist feeding frenzy" around Arday.
Sir James Cleverly said he was angry about what happened to Arday, and the university establishment - not just Cambridge - should have "done the robust due diligence and checking that should happen with any senior academic appointment".
The shadow housing secretary said he felt Arday was used as "bragging rights by some universities".
On 6 August Cambridge announced an independent investigation into Arday's appointment.
It is understood the university does not feel it right to decide on whether to proceed with its investigation.
Stand Up to Racism also organised a vigil in central London on Monday, where several speakers criticised Arday's treatment by the media.
More than 100,000 people have signed a letter to the prime minister calling for a public inquiry into the media coverage surrounding Arday before his death.
Downing Street has since declined to say "at this stage" whether the prime minister was considering an inquiry.

b523f2f94d43c98fd386ce2d.title: Cambridge University vice-chancellor heckled at Jason Arday vigil
b523f2f94d43c98fd386ce2d.author: Mousumi Bakshi; Elliot Deady
b523f2f94d43c98fd386ce2d.content:
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil in Cambridge city centre on Monday
- Published
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge was heckled as she was seen in public for the first time since the death of former professor Jason Arday.
Prof Deborah Prentice attended a vigil organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism in Cambridge city centre on Monday evening.
Shouting from a signpost in the city's market square, one attendee called Prentice "shameful" for failing to attend another event organised by Arday's students on Sunday.
Prentice previously said the university was "deeply saddened" by the academic's death.
![Dressed in a black turtle neck and trousers, Jason Arday smiles at the camera in a BBC Radio 4 studio.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/ea6e/live/9024e850-988b-11f1-83ef-33838a09c7c1.jpg)
Jason Arday was found dead in Battersea, south London, on Friday
Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
He resigned from his role at the university earlier this month after facing allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims and, in one case, had been cleared.
Asked about the heckling at the vigil, Cambridge University said: "The vice-chancellor attended the vigil to pay her respects.
"She understands that this is a very difficult time for many people. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason's family and loved ones, who have lost a father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
Concerns over media scrutiny
Arday's death sparked a debate over whether the media scrutiny was excessive or justified by his prominence.
Anger at the level of media coverage he had been subjected to was felt by many of the people who spoke to the BBC at the rally.
Addressing a crowd, Melanie Benedict, undergraduate president of Cambridge's students' union, said Arday had faced "disproportionate public scrutiny" which "would've been unbearable for anyone".
"The systemic issues that academics of colour have to face year on year have been highlighted by the tragedy of Jason's public treatment and subsequent death," they said.

Milli Akehurst's son studies law at Cambridge

"I think racism played a big part in [what happened to Arday]. He was cleared [of plagiarism], so why did it continue, and why were there so many articles within the last month or few weeks?"

Crowds gathered in Cambridge's market square as part of a vigil organised by Stand Up to Racism

"Equally, I can see parallels with people like Caroline Flack where the media go for someone and destroy them. I think there are lots of layers to this but, yes, racism is a feature of it and it would be naive to think it wasn't."

d54b73a4acbdeba9f9045702.title: Wetherspoons bans customers playing music from phones in pubs
d54b73a4acbdeba9f9045702.author: Mitchell Labiak
d54b73a4acbdeba9f9045702.content:
![A man sitting in a pub looking at his mobile phone with a pint of beer on the table in front of him](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/dbde/live/1b00c8d0-9af4-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
- Published
Wetherspoons has banned its customers from playing music out loud or taking calls on speaker, saying the noise from phones and tablets was an increasing problem driving people "nuts".
The company â which runs 792 pubs and bars across the UK â said that following complaints it has asked customers to switch their devices to silent or to use earphones.
Polling in recent years by various organisations suggests people are largely opposed to others playing music or taking calls on speaker in public spaces.
Wetherspoons told the BBC that staff would be asked to use "common sense" when enforcing the ban.
"We are not looking to ask anyone to leave a pub if they go against the ruling, but it is an option for managers if they refuse to do so," the company said.
The British Beer and Pub Association, which represents Wetherspoons and several other pub companies in the UK, said that "having a clear policy helps staff enforce rules and customers know what they can and can't do".
The group added: "We're yet to hear of anyone who relishes having a pint against the backdrop of a speakerphone call or someone loudly playing a video, so we expect this move will be greatly welcomed."
Studies suggest the majority of Britons are annoyed by hearing people take calls on speakerphone or playing videos or music on their phones without headphones.
A Transport for London survey of 1,000 people last year found 70% of respondents found loud music and phone calls without headphones a nuisance.
However, the evidence also suggests there is a clear generational gap. In an Ofcom survey of 1,010 people in August 2022, of the 13-to-17-year-olds questioned, 69% said it was acceptable to make video calls, 73% to listen to music and 83% to watch videos without headphones.
'Oasis of tranquility'
The decision by Wetherspoons follows a stricter, longstanding policy from rival pub chain Sam Smiths, which has a ban against phone or tech use of any kind, in addition to a ban on swearing.
Wetherspoons does not play music in any of its pubs, with chief executive Sir Tim Martin describing them as "an oasis of tranquillity and contemplation... in a world dominated by other people's music and amplified sound".
"In order to avoid customers being driven chicken jalfrezi by a cacophony of sound, we are kindly asking phone users to pipe down," he added.
The chain does play music in the evening at its 44 Lloyds' bars. It confirmed that the ban on customers playing music and taking calls on speaker would also apply to those venues.
The number of Wetherspoons pubs has steadily fallen over the last decade from a peak of 955 in late 2015.
The firm has faced a financial challenges during those 10 years from the Covid pandemic and inflation.
Last month, it told investors that profit for the year would be lower than expected because of higher costs for food, labour, repairs, energy and business rates.
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/d048/live/80825d90-55a8-11f1-b682-cf91850925ea.png)

Staff are instructed to use common sense, with managers having the option to ask uncooperative patrons to leave. The company, which does not normally play music in its pubs in order to maintain a quiet atmosphere, joins rival chain Sam Smiths in restricting public tech noise.

Customers are now asked to use earphones or switch devices to silent instead of playing music or taking calls on speaker.
Staff will use common sense, and managers can ask refusing customers to leave.
Surveys indicate that the general public largely finds loud phone audio in public spaces to be a nuisance, though younger demographics are more accepting of it.

da1af3f6ea4f4fbea96d0c83.title: Apple's new macOS update reportedly contains a video of AirPods with a camera | TechCrunch
da1af3f6ea4f4fbea96d0c83.author: Ivan Mehta
da1af3f6ea4f4fbea96d0c83.content:
Apple seems to be already preparing launch materials for its upcoming AirPods with a camera, a leaked video in the latest macOS update spotted by MacRumors suggests.
The video, found in macOS 26.7 RC, shows a man holding up a book and talking with Siri about it using visual information.
“With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later,” the voiceover in the video says.
MacRumous reports that these new AirPods have a camera that can be used to examine objects in front of the user and answer questions about it. The publication apparently found a line in the software code that suggests the AirPods will notify you if your hair or something else is covering the camera.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Apple was in the late stages of testing such a device. The report said the camera-equipped AirPods would look like the AirPods Pro 3, but will have a longer stem and an LED light to indicate that data is being sent to the cloud.
Other devices, like the Ray-Ban Meta Glasses, Looki pendant, and smart glasses from Rokid, already do something similar. This might be Apple’s move to embed real-world intelligence into devices before it launches smart glasses of its own.
Bloomberg noted that Apple wanted to release the new AirPods in the first half of 2026, but now that it will ship the new Siri in September, it will look to launch them along with the operating system updates.

The footage demonstrates a user utilizing Visual Intelligence to ask Siri about an object. According to reports, these upcoming AirPods may launch around the time of operating system updates.

The camera-equipped AirPods are designed to examine objects in front of the user and answer questions about them.

23bf5cceaed9195312104140.title: National Television Awards pick first all-female shortlist for drama acting award
23bf5cceaed9195312104140.author: Paul Glynn
23bf5cceaed9195312104140.content:
![A five-way split image of actors Ella Bruccoleri, Judy Parfitt, Vicky McClure, Sheridan Smith and Ruth Jones all performing separately in their NTA nominated roles](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/14f5/live/ab00e3a0-9b05-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
(Left to right) Ella Bruccoleri, Judy Parfitt, Vicky McClure, Sheridan Smith and Ruth Jones
- Published
National Television Awards voters have selected an all-female shortlist in the best drama performance category for the first time.
The five nominees include previous winner Sheridan Smith, who played campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law, and Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones for her role in Netflix thriller Run Away.
Vicky McClure gets the nod as Trigger Point's Lana Washington, while Ella Bruccoleri is shortlisted for alternative period drama The Other Bennet Sister, and Judy Parfitt is nominated for playing Sister Monica Joan in Call The Midwife.
The nominees were chosen in a public vote from an initial longlist that also included stars like David Tennant, Gary Oldman, Idris Elba, James Norton and Tom Hiddleston.
A second stage of voting is now open to pick the winners in the NTAs' 15 categories.
Elsewhere on this year's shortlists, Stacey Solomon has scored a hat-trick of nominations including best TV presenter.
That particular award was won last year by then-outgoing Match of the Day presenter Gary Lineker, breaking Ant and Dec's remarkable 23-year winning run.
Solomon will go up against the Geordie duo for this year's gong as well as Sir David Attenborough in his 100th birthday year, Traitors and chat show host Claudia Winkleman and Alison Hammond.
In the inaugural celebrity-led reality docuseries award, Solomon and her partner Joe Swash face competition from boxer Tyson Fury, Jeremy Clarkson and Emmerdale actor-turned-farmer Kelvin Fletcher, as well as funny fishermen Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse.
Mrs Brown's Boys â which this week officially cancelled its festive specials due to creator and star Brendan O'Carroll's broken jaw - has a nomination for best comedy.
Other nominated shows include Canadian breakout romance Heated Rivalry (for best new drama) - eligible as it was co-produced by Sky - and Winkleman and Tess Daly's final series of Strictly Come Dancing (for best talent show).
The NTAs, which recognise the best in British TV over the past twelve months, first launched in 1995 and the winners will be voted for by the public between now and midday on 8 September - the day of the ceremony.
Hosted again by comedian Joel Dommett, the event will take place at London's O2 arena and will be broadcast live on ITV1 and ITVX from 20:00 BST.

8791145614b455b7fb1fc3eb.content:
![A five-way split image of actors Ella Bruccoleri, Judy Parfitt, Vicky McClure, Sheridan Smith and Ruth Jones all performing separately in their NTA nominated roles](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/14f5/live/ab00e3a0-9b05-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
(Left to right) Ella Bruccoleri, Judy Parfitt, Vicky McClure, Sheridan Smith and Ruth Jones
- Published
National Television Awards voters have selected an all-female shortlist in the best drama performance category for the first time.
The five nominees include previous winner Sheridan Smith, who played campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law, and Gavin & Stacey's Ruth Jones for her role in Netflix thriller Run Away.
Vicky McClure gets the nod as Trigger Point's Lana Washington, while Ella Bruccoleri is shortlisted for alternative period drama The Other Bennet Sister, and Judy Parfitt is nominated for playing Sister Monica Joan in Call The Midwife.
The nominees were chosen in a public vote from an initial longlist that also included stars like David Tennant, Gary Oldman, Idris Elba, James Norton and Tom Hiddleston.
A second stage of voting is now open to pick the winners in the NTAs' 15 categories.
Elsewhere on this year's shortlists, Stacey Solomon has scored a hat-trick of nominations including best TV presenter.
That particular award was won last year by then-outgoing Match of the Day presenter Gary Lineker, breaking Ant and Dec's remarkable 23-year winning run.
Solomon will go up against the Geordie duo for this year's gong as well as Sir David Attenborough in his 100th birthday year, Traitors and chat show host Claudia Winkleman and Alison Hammond.
In the inaugural celebrity-led reality docuseries award, Solomon and her partner Joe Swash face competition from boxer Tyson Fury, Jeremy Clarkson and Emmerdale actor-turned-farmer Kelvin Fletcher, as well as funny fishermen Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse.
Mrs Brown's Boys â which this week officially cancelled its festive specials due to creator and star Brendan O'Carroll's broken jaw - has a nomination for best comedy.
Other nominated shows include Canadian breakout romance Heated Rivalry (for best new drama) - eligible as it was co-produced by Sky - and Winkleman and Tess Daly's final series of Strictly Come Dancing (for best talent show).
The NTAs, which recognise the best in British TV over the past twelve months, first launched in 1995 and the winners will be voted for by the public between now and midday on 8 September - the day of the ceremony.
Hosted again by comedian Joel Dommett, the event will take place at London's O2 arena and will be broadcast live on ITV1 and ITVX from 20:00 BST.

6d22d8f4a07392a7dcfc5a96.title: Babies born under sugar rationing grew into adults with lower cancer risk
6d22d8f4a07392a7dcfc5a96.author: Weilong Zhang
6d22d8f4a07392a7dcfc5a96.content:
Could how much sugar you consumed before your second birthday shape your health decades later – even into your 70s?
A new study that my colleagues and I conducted suggests the answer could be yes. People who had less sugar exposure during the first few years of life were much less likely to develop several different cancers later in life, and they also showed signs of slower biological ageing. We also found that even in adulthood, they continued to consume less sugar and had healthier diets overall.
This is not an easy question to study in real life. Researchers obviously can’t run that experiment on real babies – split them into groups, feed one group sugar, then wait 70 years to see what happens.
Britain’s postwar sugar rationing offered a rare alternative. After the second world war, sugar remained rationed in Britain for several years. But in September 1953, rationing ended and people started eating a lot more sugar. Consumption nearly doubled. This meant that children born just a few months apart had very different levels of sugar exposure both in the womb and during early childhood.
For our study, we used data from over 64,000 people born in Britain between 1951 and 1956. Those born earlier spent a larger share of their first 1,000 days under sugar rationing, while those born later experienced progressively less of it.
By the first 1,000 days, we mean the period from conception to a child’s second birthday. This is a critical stage because the body is developing very rapidly. Organs are growing, metabolism is taking shape, and the immune system is maturing.
Food and taste preferences also begin to form during this period. Although 1,000 days is a relatively short period, the effects of the food environment during this stage can last throughout a person’s life.
To track cancer cases, we used the UK Biobank – a huge health database that follows participants for decades and records, among other things, who develops cancer and when.
We found that people who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had a lower incidence of five types of cancer: breast, prostate, liver, rectal and lung cancer. The effect was strongest for liver cancer, where rates were around 69% lower, and weakest – though still substantial – for breast cancer, at 36% lower. Importantly, these differences only began to appear decades after sugar rationing had ended.
We also found that exposure to sugar rationing is related to biological ageing. Biological age is not the same as chronological age. Two people may both be 70 years old, while their cells and immune systems show different levels of ageing.
One way we measure biological ageing is through telomere length. Telomeres are protective structures located at the ends of chromosomes. As cells age, telomeres usually become shorter.
We found that people who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had longer telomeres. Based on our estimates, this difference is equivalent to about 2.2 years of slower biological ageing.
We also found lower levels of a protein called granzyme B, which rises when the immune system has been working overtime for years – another sign of slower ageing at a cellular level. Taken together, these results suggest that lower sugar exposure early in life may be related to slower ageing at the cellular level.
The sugar habit that lasted 50 years
What is most surprising, however, is not the cancer results or the biological markers of ageing. It’s how early-life sugar exposure continued to affect people’s diets even 50 years later.
We found that people who experienced sugar rationing early in life still consumed less sugar in adulthood, around age 50. They also ate less overall, and their diets were healthier and more diverse. This suggests that the level of sweetness people are exposed to very early in life may shape their taste preferences for a long time.
There appear to be two mechanisms at work. One is biological – early nutrition may shape how the metabolism, organs and immune system develop. The other is behavioural – a taste for less sweetness, formed early, seems to stick.
Other research using the end of Britain’s sugar rationing has also found that people who experienced more sugar rationing early in life had lower risks of type 2 diabetes and hypertension. A recent study using the same end of Britain’s sugar rationing found lower risks of dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, while another study reported lower risks of heart disease and stroke.
This does not mean that children should not eat sugar at all, and it certainly does not mean that postwar sugar rationing is a desirable policy. What this historical evidence shows is that, during a critical period of development, even relatively small differences in sugar exposure over a short period may leave effects that are still observable half a century later.
Children may not remember what they ate before age two. But their later health, their bodies and even their taste preferences may still carry the imprint of those very early-life experiences.
6d22d8f4a07392a7dcfc5a96.summary: A new study analyzing data from over 64,000 people born in Britain during postwar sugar rationing found that individuals exposed to less sugar during their first 1,000 days had a lower risk of several cancers, showed signs of slower biological aging, and maintained healthier diets in adulthood. The research leverages the end of sugar rationing in September 1953, which caused sugar consumption to nearly double and created distinct differences in early childhood sugar exposure. These findings indicate that early-life nutrition significantly impacts long-term health outcomes, biological aging, and lifelong taste preferences.
key_points: People who experienced longer periods of sugar rationing during their first 1,000 days had a lower incidence of breast, prostate, liver, rectal, and lung cancers later in life.
Individuals exposed to early-life sugar rationing exhibited longer telomeres and lower levels of granzyme B, indicating slower cellular aging.
Those who had less early-life sugar consumption maintained healthier, more diverse diets and consumed less sugar overall even at age 50.
The first 1,000 days from conception to age two represent a critical developmental window where diet shapes long-term metabolism, immunity, and taste preferences.

3e216c9c674811d104518fa2.title: Man in court over man's dog bite death in Wakefield
3e216c9c674811d104518fa2.author: Emily Johnson; Phil Bodmer
3e216c9c674811d104518fa2.content:
![Blue and white police tape cordons off a woodland pathway.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/0287/live/9d501050-9ac9-11f1-a74b-2f66a3b83590.jpg)
The incident happened on a disused railway line in Calder Grove, Wakefield, police say
- Published
A man has appeared in court charged with manslaughter over the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.
James Judge, 55, was left critically injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday and died in hospital at about 19:00 the same day.
Lee Ellis, also 55, of Calder Grove, appeared at Bradford Magistrates' Court on Tuesday charged with manslaughter and being in charge of a dog dangerously out of control causing injury resulting in death.
Ellis, who was described in court as a self-employed farrier, was bailed to appear at Leeds Crown Court on 16 September.
Rob Fones, representing Ellis, told the court there was "a verbal altercation in regards to right of way".
Georgina Fishwick, prosecuting, said an initial post-mortem examination had been unable to determine the exact number of dog bites to Judge.
Ellis was not asked to enter a plea to the charges, but Fones said he would be "taking the matter to trial".
Ellis, who appeared in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and tracksuit bottoms, wiped his eyes and nose with a tissue during the hearing.
A German Shepherd dog seized as part of this investigation is being held in police kennels.
3e216c9c674811d104518fa2.summary: A 55-year-old man has appeared in court charged with manslaughter and being in charge of a dangerously out of control dog following an incident in Wakefield. James Judge suffered critical injuries from a dog bite during an altercation on a disused railway line and died later that same day in the hospital. The defendant, Lee Ellis, was granted bail to appear at Leeds Crown Court in September.

Lee Ellis, 55, appeared in court charged with manslaughter and having a dangerously out of control dog.
The defense stated there was a verbal altercation regarding the right of way.
A German Shepherd dog involved in the incident has been seized and is being held in police kennels.

c98aebe7dceb9896ee060866.title: ABC sues Trump’s media regulator over demand for TV license renewals
c98aebe7dceb9896ee060866.author: Jeremy Barr
c98aebe7dceb9896ee060866.content:
ABC has sued the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), arguing that it is being retaliated against for content-based reasons in a move it warns threatens the independence of the press.
The network filed the lawsuit on Tuesday after being forced to apply early to renew its license to broadcast on the eight local television stations it owns. It is waiting to hear whether the Brendan Carr-led FCC approves its renewal requests, or, more likely, holds a hearing on their merits.
Late last month, a group of prominent former FCC officials, including key staffers and commissioners appointed by both Democratic and Republican presidents, issued a warning – in a filing – that the agency is trying to send a “chilling message” to broadcasters after forcing ABC to apply early.
Conservative organizations, including the Center for American Rights and the Media Research Center, filed petitions urging the FCC to deny the renewals, arguing that the network’s journalism is politically biased. ABC also still faces an FCC investigation over the daytime talkshow The View for a potential violation of equal time rules, an inquiry that remains open.
“Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the network said in the suit, filed on behalf of its eight local stations in district court for the District of Columbia.
“That campaign began in this Administration’s earliest days and has only intensified since. Again and again, the Administration has attacked ABC’s speech – the stories its journalists report and the viewpoints its network programs air. Over time, those attacks have escalated into express demands that ABC be stripped of its broadcast licenses because of its speech.”
The lawsuit makes clear that ABC does not expect the FCC to renew its licenses, posing an existential threat to the network.
“The Commission is poised to make good on its threat any day now: the public comment period on the renewal applications has closed, and the Commission may, at any moment, issue an unprecedented Hearing Designation Order for all eight Stations, which would kick off a formal agency adjudication to determine the fate of ABC’s licenses.”
The network said that any adjudication process over its licenses would be a “charade”, particularly because the agency cannot, by statute, grant license renewals several years early.
“The Commission cannot lawfully grant renewal this early in the license terms – the only outcomes on the table are adverse to Plaintiffs,” the network said in the lawsuit, expressing concern that the FCC would either “prolong” the process, “miring ABC in years of costly litigation”, or deny it altogether.
“In either scenario, the Administration accomplishes its goal of eliminating a perceived media critic: either it gets Plaintiffs to fall in line, or it silences them if they refuse,” the plaintiffs argued.
ABC’s lawyers argued that, if left unchecked, the Trump administration would have the ability to retaliate against any media company they dislike for editorial and political purposes. “If the Administration gets its way, the message to every media company in the country will be unmistakable: tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government,” they wrote. “In such a world, the press could in no way be described as free.”
The network asked the court to stop the FCC from taking any actions against it or threatening any actions against it.
The Guardian has approached ABC for comment on the lawsuit.
An FCC spokesperson said: “All broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest—even Disney. The FCC has been examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination for over a year. Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC’s proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters. The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead.”
Gigi Sohn, who served as counselor to the chairman of the FCC during Barack Obama’s administration, said the lawsuit was a major step in the effort to fight back against the administration’s regulatory overreaches.
“For months, the FCC has waged a campaign of censorship and control against Disney’s ABC stations, using the threat of broadcast license revocations to punish a company for speech this administration doesn’t like. I have long called on companies to push back against this kind of government intimidation, and I’m glad Disney has shown courage and stepped up. This should be a welcome sign for every broadcaster who has felt the weight of this overreaching government pressure in silence,” she said.
“I am hopeful that this will mark the beginning of the end of this administration’s disregard for the Constitution and the law, and that the coming months will bring the costly legal defeat this agency has been asking for since it started down this path.”
c98aebe7dceb9896ee060866.summary: ABC has filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the US district court for the District of Columbia, accusing the agency of retaliating against its content and threatening press independence. The network was forced to apply early to renew licenses for its eight local television stations following petitions from conservative groups and ongoing investigations. ABC argues that the FCC's actions are designed to punish the network for its journalism and political viewpoints.
key_points: ABC sued the FCC after being forced to submit early broadcast license renewals for its eight local TV stations.
The network alleges the administration is waging a retaliatory campaign to punish ABC for its broadcast content and journalism.
Conservative organizations previously filed petitions urging the FCC to deny the renewals due to alleged political bias.
An FCC spokesperson stated the agency is examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination and must operate in the public interest.
ABC's lawsuit warns that the administration's actions threaten the independence of a free press nationwide.

“The Commission cannot lawfully grant renewal this early in the license terms – the only outcomes on the table are adverse to Plaintiffs,” the network said in the lawsuit, expressing concern that the FCC would either “prolong” the process, “miring ABC in years of costly litigation”, or deny it altogether.
“In either scenario, the Administration accomplishes its goal of eliminating a perceived media critic: either it gets Plaintiffs to fall in line, or it silences them if they refuse,” the plaintiffs argued.
ABC’s lawyers argued that, if left unchecked, the Trump administration would have the ability to retaliate against any media company they dislike for editorial and political purposes. “If the Administration gets its way, the message to every media company in the country will be unmistakable: tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government,” they wrote. “In such a world, the press could in no way be described as free.”
The network asked the court to stop the FCC from taking any actions against it or threatening any actions against it.
The Guardian has approached ABC for comment on the lawsuit.
An FCC spokesperson said: “All broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest—even Disney. The FCC has been examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination for over a year. Disney is obviously very concerned about the FCC’s proceeding, as evidenced by their ongoing campaign of disinformation as well as their decision to ask a court to stop the FCC from further pursuing matters. The FCC will continue to follow the facts and law wherever they lead.”
Gigi Sohn, who served as counselor to the chairman of the FCC during Barack Obama’s administration, said the lawsuit was a major step in the effort to fight back against the administration’s regulatory overreaches.
“For months, the FCC has waged a campaign of censorship and control against Disney’s ABC stations, using the threat of broadcast license revocations to punish a company for speech this administration doesn’t like. I have long called on companies to push back against this kind of government intimidation, and I’m glad Disney has shown courage and stepped up. This should be a welcome sign for every broadcaster who has felt the weight of this overreaching government pressure in silence,” she said.
“I am hopeful that this will mark the beginning of the end of this administration’s disregard for the Constitution and the law, and that the coming months will bring the costly legal defeat this agency has been asking for since it started down this path.”
dd7d493a6238eb6e9a2db7de.summary: ABC has filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the US district court for the District of Columbia, accusing the agency of retaliating against its content and threatening press independence. The network was forced to apply early to renew licenses for its eight local television stations following petitions from conservative groups and ongoing investigations. ABC argues that the FCC's actions are designed to punish the network for its journalism and political viewpoints.
key_points: ABC sued the FCC after being forced to submit early broadcast license renewals for its eight local TV stations.
The network alleges the administration is waging a retaliatory campaign to punish ABC for its broadcast content and journalism.
Conservative organizations previously filed petitions urging the FCC to deny the renewals due to alleged political bias.
An FCC spokesperson stated the agency is examining claims that Disney engaged in illegal DEI discrimination and must operate in the public interest.
ABC's lawsuit warns that the administration's actions threaten the independence of a free press nationwide.

3cea257673013f2004e64951.title: Why is feeding deer in The Royal Parks a problem?
3cea257673013f2004e64951.author: Jess Warren
3cea257673013f2004e64951.content:
![A sign at Richmond Park telling visitors not to feed the deer.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/3505/live/268038a0-9aed-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
Visitors to London's Royal Parks are being reminded that it is illegal , externalto feed the wild deer after a man was injured by a stag that approached his picnic group.
From safety risks to photographing deer responsibly, here is what you need to know about the deer in Richmond Park and Bushy Park.
Why are people being told not to feed the deer?
Visitors to south-west London's Richmond and Bushy parks are being urged not to feed the red and fallow deer or get within 50m (165ft) of the animals.
On Saturday, a man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag in Richmond Park when it approached his picnic group.
The deer was subsequently shot by a Royal Parks wildlife officer as it was deemed a danger to visitors.
![A black and white image taken in September 1936 of a visitor to Richmond Park reading a Royal Parks notice warning people about "Danger from Deer".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9684/live/e42dcba0-9ae9-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors to Richmond and Bushy parks have been told for decades not to feed the deer
Paul Richards, park manager at Richmond Park, said the animal's behaviour was likely the direct result of having previously been fed by visitors at the park.
"It is only because people had fed this particular animal that its behaviour had changed," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
The "do not feed" warning is not new. The Royal Parks has regularly told people visiting both of the south-west London parks not to feed the wild animals.
How can feeding deer put people at risk?
The deer in both parks are wild animals, and can act unpredictably around humans.
Unlike deer in other places, such as the city of Nara in Japan where deer are regularly fed by people, London's deer should not be approached or fed.
Richards said the deer in The Royal Parks had begun to associate visitors with food, which was "not their natural behaviour".
"Enjoy the deer, respect the deer, keep a safe distance from the deer," he said.
"Don't feed them, they don't need feeding. Some people think they're doing a good deed. In fact you're not, you're doing quite the opposite."
Richards said that if fed, the deer began to associate people with food and would be more likely to approach groups or individuals in the park.
This, he warned, was dangerous to visitors and put them at risk of serious injury.
Feeding deer may also increase the risk of them ingesting plastic, which blocks their stomachs and causes malnutrition.
My children want to pet the deer, why is that not allowed?
Last month, families with young children were seen trying to stroke the deer in Richmond Park.
Richards said his team were "shocked and extremely concerned" by video footage from the park, and called the actions "deeply irresponsible and highly dangerous".
The park manager explained that closing in on the animals would cause the deer stress and risked a "fatal incident".
"Richmond Park's red and fallow deer are wild, powerful animals. Although they may appear calm, they can react suddenly and aggressively if they feel threatened," he said.
"Stags can weigh more than 25 stone (159kg) and run at speeds of up to 30mph (48km/h), making them highly dangerous if visitors get too close."
Do the deer have enough food in the drought?
Red and fallow deer eat grasses, leaves and shoots of trees, as well as acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts.
Richards said: "They don't need to be fed. A lot of people are thinking: 'It's bone dry out there, everything is brown', but the deer don't need supplementary feeding here at Richmond Park."
![A deer reaching up to eat leaves from a tree in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b83e/live/d7565f30-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Deer eat grasses, leaves, acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts
"There's plenty of things for them to eat," he added. "They're grazing on bramble, we're already seeing a bit of an early autumn, and it won't be long before sweet chestnuts are beginning to fall, so there is plenty of food for them."
Visitors are urged not to remove conkers (horse chestnuts) from the park as they are a vital part of the deer's diet and help to build up their fat reserves for winter.
How can I photograph the deer?
London's deer population is much-loved and photographed, due to their apparent juxtaposition with city-life.
The current 630-strong herd of wild red and fallow deer in Richmond Park were first introduced by Charles I in 1637 and roam freely amongst the trees and grasslands.
They have been enjoyed by visitors for decades, but must be respected, Richards said.
![A woman stands beneath a tree to photograph stags in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/869/cpsprodpb/775b/live/64f843e0-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors are told to photograph deer through a zoom lens
"The deer here are wild, they have been here for centuries," he said.
"If you want to photograph them, photograph them using the zoom function on your phone or camera."
He said visitors must keep a distance of 50m (165ft) from the animals.
What should you do if a deer approaches you in a Royal Park?
Visitors are told to never feed or touch the deer in Richmond and Bushy parks.
If one comes towards you, put all food and packaging out of sight and move away slowly and calmly, The Royal Parks says.
People should not try to move the deer away themselves.
"If you witness someone putting themselves, others or the deer at risk, please do not try and intervene but report it immediately to the police," a Royal Parks spokesperson says.

3cea257673013f2004e64951.summary: Visitors to London's Richmond and Bushy parks are legally prohibited from feeding the wild deer because it alters their behavior and creates safety risks. A recent incident involving a man injured by a stag led to the animal being shot, highlighting the dangers of approaching or feeding the park's wildlife. Park officials stress that the deer have sufficient natural food sources and urge the public to maintain a distance of at least 50 meters.
key_points: Feeding the wild deer in Richmond and Bushy parks is illegal.
A man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag that approached his picnic group, leading to the animal being shot.
Feeding causes deer to associate humans with food, leading them to approach visitors and increasing the risk of plastic ingestion.
Visitors are advised to keep a distance of 50 meters, avoid petting or feeding the animals, and use zoom lenses for photography.

ebfe87da1e804ba5d0e1d203.title: Everything you need to know about the Wessex Water hosepipe ban
ebfe87da1e804ba5d0e1d203.author: Clara Bullock
ebfe87da1e804ba5d0e1d203.content:
Hear from Wessex Water's head of water supply
- Published
Water restrictions have come into force for 1.4 million people after a water company introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years.
Wessex Water, which supplies water to people in Bath, parts of Somerset,â¯Dorsetâ¯and Wiltshire, has taken the decision after the region was formally declared as being in drought.
It comes after several water companies across the country, including Thames Water and South West Water, introduced bans.
Bristol Water and Severn Trent Water have yet to announce restrictions.
But what does a hosepipe ban entail and what can you do to reduce your water use? We have you covered.
More from Somerset
What does the hosepipe ban mean practically?
Temporarily, the ban means households are no longer permitted to use a hosepipe.
This includes for activities such as watering gardens, washing cars, patios, paths and driveways, cleaning windows and filling swimming and paddling pools.
The ban is in effect across Bath and parts of Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire, as well as Berkeley, Sharpness and Wotton-under-Edge in Gloucestershire.
How did people cope with the 1976 heatwave?
Why did Wessex Water put the ban in place?
The ban marks the first time in 50 years that Wessex Water has introduced restrictions on water use, the last time being the famous drought of 1976.
The nation recorded its driest July since records began in 1836.
Wessex Water chief executive Ruth Jefferson said the decision to put a ban in place comes from a higher demand for water during the exceptionally hot and dry summer.
![A track runs through dry fields, with hills visible in the distance. The landscape is cast in an orange light, at sunset.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/25bd/live/5d2228b0-8b6a-11f1-9c48-75e854e5573d.jpg)
One hosepipe ban has already been introduced previously by Thames Water
Jefferson said: "The prolonged and extreme dry weather has meant demand across our region hasâ¯consistently remainedâ¯at more than 400 million litres per day, 30% above average for this time of year and the equivalent of almost half a million hosepipes running for a full hour every day.
"While we're not running out of water for essential use, our challenge has beenâ¯movingâ¯water through theâ¯networkâ¯quickly enough to meetâ¯these record levels of demand," she added.
![Water is scattered across a field of crops with trees in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/2f90/live/ed231120-89aa-11f1-b8ee-9b3c26ad07bb.jpg)
Farmers are running out of water as the area remains in drought conditions
Are there exemptions?
There are a few exceptions to the rule, to protect vulnerable people.
These include:
- physical impairments or restricted hand movement
- stairlift, hoist or electric bed users
- respiratory conditions that require the use of a ventilator
- other chronic or serious illnesses such as Parkinsons, MS, MND, cancer, stroke, organ failure or severe arthritis
Is it against the law to break the ban?
Yes, the ban is a legal restriction on water use set out in the Water Industry Act.
Water companies can legally enforce these rules during periods of drought or severe water shortage to protect public water supplies.
Breaking the ban is a criminal offence and can carry a fine of up to Â£1,000.
What can you do to reduce your water usage?
There are a few things households can do to further reduce the use of water, including:
- Lettingâ¯theâ¯lawn go brownâ¯â it will recover when the rain comes
- Using a watering can to water plants
- Reusingâ¯washing up water for patio pots and movingâ¯pots intoâ¯the shadeâ¯so theyâ¯dry out less
- Filling up paddling pools using buckets or watering cans and coveringâ¯themâ¯when not in use to prevent evaporation
- Keeping showers shortâ¯andâ¯notâ¯leavingâ¯taps running whileâ¯brushing teeth orâ¯doingâ¯the dishes
- Not washing the car, just keep the windscreen and number plate clean.
Jefferson said: "We know so many of our customers have already been taking steps to save water and we're incredibly grateful for their support so far this summer. It makes such a difference."
ebfe87da1e804ba5d0e1d203.summary: Wessex Water has introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years, affecting 1.4 million people after the region was formally declared in a drought. The restriction prohibits activities like watering gardens, washing cars, and filling pools due to record water demand driven by exceptionally hot and dry weather. Breaking the ban is a criminal offence under the Water Industry Act and can result in a fine of up to £1,000, though exemptions exist for vulnerable individuals.
key_points: Wessex Water's hosepipe ban affects 1.4 million people in Bath, parts of Somerset, Dorset, Wiltshire, and Gloucestershire.
The ban prohibits using hosepipes for gardens, cars, patios, windows, and filling pools.
Water demand has remained 30% above average due to prolonged extreme dry weather.
Breaking the hosepipe ban is a criminal offence that carries a fine of up to £1,000.
Exemptions to the ban are available for individuals with specific physical impairments or serious illnesses.

94afc58d0512ac09ffa67af5.title: Streetwear Brand Supreme’s Fall/Winter Catalog Has Collabs With Analogue Pocket, Dyson Vacuums, and Retro Kodak Cameras
94afc58d0512ac09ffa67af5.author: Bo Moore
94afc58d0512ac09ffa67af5.content:
Streetwear brand Supreme has unveiled its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, and it features a collab with Analogue Pocket, the fantastic retro handheld that lets you play your Game Boy cartridges on FPGA-based hardware.
Also in the collection is a Supreme-branded Dyson Vacuum, Kodak Super-8 Camera, and a galvanized steel mailbox, all bright red, of course.
The Analogue Pocket collab actually comes in two variants: one the standard Supreme red, as well as a second that's plated in 24K gold. As for the underlying Analogue Pocket itself, it's the same high-end retro handheld we loved in our review, which my colleague Seth noted "solves the limitations of classic handhelds with a familiar but distinct style you don't find with emulation-based solutions."
The Pocket uses an FPGA solution, short for "field-programmable gate arrays," which means it replicates the Game Boy and Game Boy Advance's original electronic hardware "at the transistor level." In other words, games are played on actual hardware, rather than being emulated, so every game – from Kirby Tilt n' Tumble's original motion controls to Perfect Dark's AAA-powered rumble pak – runs exactly as it was originally intended.
"Simply put," Seth said, "it's the best possible way to enjoy your handheld gaming collection."
The standard edition Analogue Pocket retails for $239.99, though it comes in limited quantities and typically sells out quickly whenever units become available. There's no word yet how much the new Supreme-branded variant will cost, but it will undoubtedly be even more limited edition.
For other, likely less expensive ways to play your games on the go, be sure to check our guide to the best handheld gaming PCs.
Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

The Analogue Pocket comes in standard Supreme red and a 24K gold-plated variant. The device uses FPGA hardware to authentically play Game Boy and Game Boy Advance cartridges without emulation.
key_points: Supreme unveiled its Fall/Winter 2026 collection featuring high-profile collaborations.
Collabs include a Dyson Vacuum, Kodak Super-8 Camera, galvanized steel mailbox, and the Analogue Pocket.
The Analogue Pocket collaboration is available in standard Supreme red and a 24K gold-plated version.
The Analogue Pocket replicates original Game Boy hardware at the transistor level using FPGA technology.

The Analogue Pocket collab actually comes in two variants: one the standard Supreme red, as well as a second that's plated in 24K gold. As for the underlying Analogue Pocket itself, it's the same high-end retro handheld we loved in our review, which my colleague Seth noted "solves the limitations of classic handhelds with a familiar but distinct style you don't find with emulation-based solutions."
The Pocket uses an FPGA solution, short for "field-programmable gate arrays," which means it replicates the Game Boy and Game Boy Advance's original electronic hardware "at the transistor level." In other words, games are played on actual hardware, rather than being emulated, so every game – from Kirby Tilt n' Tumble's original motion controls to Perfect Dark's AAA-powered rumble pak – runs exactly as it was originally intended.
"Simply put," Seth said, "it's the best possible way to enjoy your handheld gaming collection."
The standard edition Analogue Pocket retails for $239.99, though it comes in limited quantities and typically sells out quickly whenever units become available. There's no word yet how much the new Supreme-branded variant will cost, but it will undoubtedly be even more limited edition.
For other, likely less expensive ways to play your games on the go, be sure to check our guide to the best handheld gaming PCs.

The Analogue Pocket comes in standard Supreme red and a 24K gold-plated variant. The device uses FPGA hardware to authentically play Game Boy and Game Boy Advance cartridges without emulation.
