3385e7c63d2e4dfb85bb599e.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua negotiations enter critical week with ongoing talks about staging fight in New York
3385e7c63d2e4dfb85bb599e.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua negotiations enter critical week with ongoing talks about staging fight in New York
Tyson Fury has teased an Anthony Joshua fight announcement on social media; The British heavyweight rivals are yet to finalise terms for a fight; Anthony Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn is keen for the bout to be held in the UK but New York is now being discussed as a location
Tuesday 18 August 2026 14:25, UK
Negotiations for the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight have entered a 'critical week' with talks ongoing about staging the heavyweight clash in New York.
The British stars are set to finally share the ring this year, although an official announcement has been delayed over discussion about the location of the fight, with Madison Square Garden now emerging as the likely venue.
Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn has revealed how the original fight contract stipulated that the bout would be staged in the UK, but fresh negotiations are taking place amid growing optimism that the blockbuster battle will be confirmed for later this year.
- Latest boxing headlines, reports, highlights and interviews
- Boxing in 2026: Key dates, results and upcoming schedule
- Get Sky Sports or stream boxing and more with no contract
Frank Smith, Matchroom Boxing CEO, told Sky Sports: "It will disappointing for it not to be in the UK, but at the same time if it means seeing the fight, we all want to see that fight happen. Let's see how things play out.
"There's obviously been suggestions and discussions about New York. AJ has fought there before. AJ has fought all around the world. We're following the terms of what we signed up to right now, which is a fight in the UK. That is what we signed up to and when the fight was announced in March, April time, the fight was signed, those were the terms we signed up for.
"They are the conversations really that are taking place right now. MSG is a proposed venue that they would like to look at, i.e The Ring Magazine, Saudi delegation, so let's see.
"I think November is possible. Later in November is possible, but again the next seven to 10 days, a lot of progress has got to be made in order to make that happen to get [fighters] into camp to give yourself that eight to 10 week period, a dedicated camp away from all the promotional obligations.
"The pressure is on over the next week to get it done."
Asked if the next week is 'critical', Smith added: "I would say 100 per cent. It's never easy putting timeframes on things but when it comes to the date of it actually happening, the next week or so we need to get things together."
Both fighters sharpened their skills in warm-up fights last month as Fury sealed a seventh-round stoppage of Mariusz Wach before Joshua knocked out Kristian Prenga after recovering from an early knockdown.
"We're all focused on making it happen," said Smith. "We're all focused on getting the final details together but some work still to be done.
"Lots of discussions ongoing. Lots of conversations happening right now. I'm confident that the fight will happen.
"I'm very confident we will see that fight and AJ will knock out Tyson Fury this year."
Fury teases AJ fight 'It's the one you've all been waiting for!
Fury had earlier teased that a fight announcement was 'imminent', a few hours after Netflix had run a promotional video during its WWE coverage with the closing tagline that the event was 'coming soon.'
Speaking on his official Instagram, Fury had said: "Everything is going well. I've got some big news going to be dropped very soon. All is good in the hood. Big fight on the horizon.
"It's the one you've all been waiting for about to be announced imminently, so stay tuned."
3385e7c63d2e4dfb85bb599e.summary: Negotiations for the heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have entered a critical week, with discussions focusing on potentially staging the bout in New York at Madison Square Garden. Although the original contract stipulated a UK location, promoter representatives indicate that the next seven to 10 days are crucial for finalizing terms, securing a venue, and setting a possible date in late November.
key_points: Negotiations for the Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight have reached a critical stage over the next week to ten days.
Talks are currently underway to potentially stage the bout in New York at Madison Square Garden.
Eddie Hearn and Matchroom Boxing originally signed terms for the fight to take place in the UK.
Matchroom Boxing CEO Frank Smith stated that a late November date is possible if a deal is finalized soon.
Both fighters recently secured victories in warm-up fights last month.

That is what we signed up to and when the fight was announced in March, April time, the fight was signed, those were the terms we signed up for.
"They are the conversations really that are taking place right now. MSG is a proposed venue that they would like to look at, i.e The Ring Magazine, Saudi delegation, so let's see.
"I think November is possible. Later in November is possible, but again the next seven to 10 days, a lot of progress has got to be made in order to make that happen to get [fighters] into camp to give yourself that eight to 10 week period, a dedicated camp away from all the promotional obligations.
"The pressure is on over the next week to get it done."
Asked if the next week is 'critical', Smith added: "I would say 100 per cent. It's never easy putting timeframes on things but when it comes to the date of it actually happening, the next week or so we need to get things together."
Both fighters sharpened their skills in warm-up fights last month as Fury sealed a seventh-round stoppage of Mariusz Wach before Joshua knocked out Kristian Prenga after recovering from an early knockdown.
"We're all focused on making it happen," said Smith. "We're all focused on getting the final details together but some work still to be done.
"Lots of discussions ongoing. Lots of conversations happening right now. I'm confident that the fight will happen.
"I'm very confident we will see that fight and AJ will knock out Tyson Fury this year."
Fury teases AJ fight 'It's the one you've all been waiting for!
Fury had earlier teased that a fight announcement was 'imminent', a few hours after Netflix had run a promotional video during its WWE coverage with the closing tagline that the event was 'coming soon.'
Speaking on his official Instagram, Fury had said: "Everything is going well. I've got some big news going to be dropped very soon. All is good in the hood. Big fight on the horizon.
"It's the one you've all been waiting for about to be announced imminently, so stay tuned."
405d76dce6386b645e9fe541.summary: Negotiations for the heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have entered a critical week, with discussions focusing on potentially staging the bout in New York at Madison Square Garden. Although the original contract stipulated a UK location, promoter representatives indicate that the next seven to 10 days are crucial for finalizing terms, securing a venue, and setting a possible date in late November.

e4d5c3ce5b2989eb771c228d.title: After a long wait: the Premier League breaks its silence over the Manchester City case | Goal.com
e4d5c3ce5b2989eb771c228d.author: Khaled Mahmoud
e4d5c3ce5b2989eb771c228d.content:
Richard Masters, the chief executive of the Premier League, has admitted the verdict in Manchester City's financial charges case "has taken longer than expected". He also insisted he remains fully committed to keeping the proceedings confidential until a final decision is reached.
The case dates back three years. The Premier League charged the Sky Blues with breaching financial fair play rules across nine seasons, specifically the period from 2009 to 2018, during which the club lifted three Premier League titles. City's hierarchy have flatly denied every charge and rejected any suggestion of wrongdoing.
At the heart of the case is an alleged failure to provide accurate financial information to the league over those nine years, along with a refusal to cooperate with the investigations into the club's finances. Both parties sat through hearings that ran for 12 weeks before an independent three-member commission between September and December of 2024. Nearly two years on, no verdict has landed.
Quizzed on the latest developments during the launch event for the new Premier League season (2026-2027), Masters told the Sky News network: "There is nothing I can add at the present time. Our rules are entirely clear on this matter, and I must keep everything confidential until we are ready to issue the decision and announce it with full clarity."
By way of explanation, the chief executive added: "I cannot provide any updates regarding the timing or the progress of the procedures. The only path available to us is to let the legal process take its natural course. I fully understand the frustration that exists, as the matter has indeed taken longer than expected."
![Manchester City crest](https://cdn.sportfeeds.io/sdl/images/team/crest/medium/YaWwRy_S6TKMuwJHBvDbR.png?quality=60&auto=webp&format=pjpg)
![AFC Bournemouth crest](https://cdn.sportfeeds.io/sdl/images/team/crest/medium/FS7UO4BdZPMJrL5MlqxyL.png?quality=60&auto=webp&format=pjpg)
Was he angry at the length of the deliberations? Masters said not. "Of course not. I previously stated that the commission needs the time and sufficient space to carry out its work. In the end, the role of the Premier League is limited to bringing the charges, when sufficient evidence is available, before an independent commission to enable it to establish the truth, which is something that should not be constrained by the length of time it takes to reach that truth."
e4d5c3ce5b2989eb771c228d.summary: Premier League Chief Executive Richard Masters has acknowledged that the financial charges case against Manchester City has taken longer than expected. Masters reaffirmed his commitment to maintaining confidentiality regarding the proceedings until an independent commission reaches a final decision. Manchester City denies all allegations of breaching financial fair play rules across the nine-season period in question.
key_points: Premier League CEO Richard Masters admitted the Manchester City financial case is taking longer than expected.
Manchester City was charged with breaching financial fair play rules across nine seasons from 2009 to 2018.
The club denies all charges and any suggestion of financial wrongdoing.
Masters confirmed that proceedings will remain strictly confidential until a final decision is issued by the independent commission.

93be2a8804adfc2f6c7c9de4.title: Our Survival Might One Day Rely on Nuking a 'City Killer' Asteroid. Scientists Just Tested Whether It'll Work
93be2a8804adfc2f6c7c9de4.author: Michelle Starr
93be2a8804adfc2f6c7c9de4.content:
If an asteroid above a certain size ever gets close enough to Earth, humanity may be in serious trouble.
Even a relatively small space rock – around the size of a football field – would be large enough to completely destroy a city.
Because some are so dark and non-reflective, asteroids can be hard to spot, too, and it's not like we can just put up a shield that will gently deflect asteroids away.
So how do we stop an asteroid from wreaking destruction on Earth? Well, one potential method that sounds straight out of science fiction but could actually work would be to wallop it with the most powerful weapon humanity has ever devised – a nuclear warhead.
Now, we can't actually test this easily. Nukes aren't exactly lying around waiting for someone to chuck them at asteroids, and hauling a spacecraft to an asteroid isn't a walk in the park to boot.
So, in a new simulation, a team led by astrophysicist Isaiah Santistevan of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the US pitted a 1-megaton nuke against a 160-meter (525-foot) city-killer asteroid.
And the cockamamie thing is that it could actually work – but absolutely not in the way you're probably thinking.
"Based on the extent of damage, the directionality of the material motion, and the [velocity change] that we impart on these asteroids, we suggest that disruption is highly likely for two of the three scenarios," the researchers write in a paper in The Planetary Science Journal.
"Simulations such as these help to further inform the viability of nuclear mitigation options for planetary defense and support emergency response planning."
The idea of nuking an asteroid has been around for decades, and you probably imagine it would involve detonating a device sitting on – or even under – the surface to either blow the rock to smithereens or impart enough momentum to kick it off its current trajectory.
It makes sense, right? But the problem is, there's no guarantee the asteroid itself would play ball.
An asteroid doesn't present a simple, stationary target; it can tumble and rotate through space. Getting a spacecraft to one is doable, but difficult; it's far harder to land on the surface, stay there, and start drilling.
Fortunately, as the new work shows, the nuke doesn't have to touch the asteroid at all. Its detonation can take place several meters from the asteroid surface.
That sounds counterintuitive. Space is an effective vacuum; there's insufficient medium to carry a shockwave, even from a megaton warhead, even at a distance of just 10 meters.
But the shockwave is not the mechanism that can alter the asteroid here.
Instead, it's X-rays – scads and scads of blazing X-rays.
Around 70 to 80 percent of the energy produced by a nuclear explosive can emerge as X-rays, and it's this radiation that would sear the asteroid's surface.
"These X-rays deposit energy in a thin surface layer of the asteroid, driving vaporization and ablation," the researchers explain.
"The vaporized material expands, and if it can overcome the local gravitational field, it is ejected, which imparts a change in momentum that alters the asteroid's velocity."
![Scientists Simulated Nuking a 'City Killer' Asteroid. Here's What Happened.](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/blooooosh.jpg)
It's not dissimilar to the way material escaping a comet imparts momentum that can change the spin of the comet's nucleus – think of the way a garden hose jumps and twists when the escaping water pressure is high enough.
But for a nuked asteroid, there's an additional effect.
The sudden blast of X-ray energy also drives a powerful shock wave into the asteroid itself, where it can crack and fracture the rock from within.
It was this last part that particularly intrigued the researchers. It's possible that, one day, an asteroid is discovered that is too large or spotted too late for simply nudging aside to be a viable strategy.
So, they ran three detailed 3D simulations, using the shape and porous structure of asteroid Bennu (upon which NASA landed a spacecraft in 2020) as a realistic basis for their simulated space rock.
They tweaked parameters such as the distance of detonation and how easily the asteroid fractured under the X-ray-induced stress.
For this, they used fracture models based on two real space rocks: the Chelyabinsk meteorite, which exploded over Russia in 2013, and the Aba Panu meteorite, which fell in Nigeria in 2018.
In the longest simulation, with the bomb 10 meters above the surface, 98.2 percent of the asteroid material became fully damaged, and roughly 97 percent was moving faster than the asteroid's escape velocity. Large portions were also moving sideways in opposite directions – basically showing the asteroid pulling itself apart.
When they moved the bomb farther away, to 25 meters, things got even weirder.
![Scientists Simulated Nuking a 'City Killer' Asteroid. Here's What Happened.](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/asteroid-comparison.jpg)
Less nuclear energy actually reached the asteroid, but the X-rays illuminated a larger area of its surface – a bit like pulling a flashlight away illuminates a larger area with a slightly dimmer beam.
But that beam produced more widespread damage: after 68 milliseconds, 92.6 percent of the asteroid was fully damaged, compared with 78.1 percent in the equivalent 10-meter simulation at the same point in time.
That suggests that zooming the nuke in as close as possible may not always be the best strategy for disrupting an asteroid.
Before we get too carried away, there's a catch.
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
The simulations were extremely computationally expensive. The longest one, which followed just 145 milliseconds of action, took 59 days to run on 1,680 computer processors.
This means that the researchers could not determine the long-term fate of the disrupted asteroid.
It could have broken up and the pieces dispersed safely; it could have fragmented into smaller pieces that were still large enough to pose a threat; or the asteroid could have managed to bind itself back together gravitationally after a pebbly shrug.
Still, the work represents a significant step towards working out whether nuclear weapons really could work as an effective last line of defense against an Earth-bound asteroid.
"These results are a step toward the immensely difficult problem of doing comprehensive nuclear mitigation modeling for planetary defense scenarios," the researchers write.
"High-fidelity simulations such as the ones presented here allow us to continue pushing the limits of what is possible."
The findings have been published in The Planetary Science Journal.
93be2a8804adfc2f6c7c9de4.summary: Researchers recently used 3D simulations to test whether a 1-megaton nuclear warhead could successfully disrupt a 160-meter "city-killer" asteroid. Instead of relying on a physical impact or shockwave in the vacuum of space, the detonation would blast the asteroid's surface with X-rays, causing vaporization and internal fracturing that alters its velocity. The simulations demonstrated that detonating the weapon several meters away from the surface could effectively fracture and disrupt the asteroid, though long-term tracking of the resulting fragments remains a challenge.
key_points: A team led by astrophysicist Isaiah Santistevan simulated using a 1-megaton nuclear warhead against a 160-meter asteroid modeled after Bennu.
The nuclear detonation does not need to touch the asteroid; instead, intense X-rays sear the surface, driving vaporization and ablation to change the rock's momentum.
Simulations showed that X-rays also create internal shock waves that crack and fracture the asteroid from within.
Detonating the bomb 25 meters away illuminated a larger surface area with X-rays, resulting in more widespread initial damage than a closer 10-meter detonation.
Long-term outcomes—such as whether disrupted pieces will safely disperse or reassemble gravitationally—remain unknown due to the high computational cost of the simulations.

731bf3916bed3b84605d53a0.title: Bowel cancer cases in under-50s at record high in Scotland
731bf3916bed3b84605d53a0.author: Aimee Stanton; Susie Forrest
731bf3916bed3b84605d53a0.content:
![Anona Gauld is wearing a pink and black spotty shirt and black glasses. She is smiling and there is a 40th birthday cake in front of her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/0751/live/be585630-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld had just turned 40 when she was diagnosed with cancer
- Published
The number of people under the age of 50 being diagnosed with bowel cancer in Scotland has reached a record high, with almost 290 new cases in 2024, new figures show.
Bowel cancer is the fourth most common cancer in Scotland and is more often diagnosed in older people, with those over 50 offered screening in an attempt to detect it early.
However, new figures from Public Health Scotland, external show incidence has jumped by 38% in the under-50s over the past decade, with rates among younger women increasing by 56% in comparison with 24% in younger men.
Last month, the Scottish government asked the UK National screening committee to look at lowering the age for bowel screening to 45, to target younger patients.
Anona Gauld is one of a growing number of women under 50 being diagnosed with colorectal cancer, the medical name for bowel cancers.
She told the BBC her journey towards diagnosis started when she turned 40 in March 2023 and couldn't manage a birthday glass of fizz.
She'd had a mysterious pain in her shoulder for several weeks, which got worse every time she drank alcohol.
Gauld, from Stonehaven, thought she'd pulled a muscle or had been lying awkwardly in bed but by August she had been diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer, which had spread to her liver.
![Anona Gauld is wearing a white shirt and black glasses. She has mid length brown hair and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/422a/live/d22e2810-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer
She had been going back and forth to her GP over several months but believes cancer wasn't initially considered, partly because of her age.
"One doctor even told me it was because my bra was too tight," she said.
"It was just a mystery."
Doctors later said the pain in her shoulder was actually coming from her liver, where they discovered a 13cm (5in) secondary tumour which had spread from her bowel.
![Lathan is sat in the driver's seat of the car and is smiling at the cancer. Anona is sat next to him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8857/live/cce81140-9af2-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Anona has three children aged between 15 and 21
"It was a big shock," Gauld says.
"I was young, I was healthy. I had a healthy diet and you don't think it's going to happen to you."
She had chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and then surgery on her liver and bowel in 2024.
Last year the cancer came back in her liver, and since then she's been back on treatment.
"People can have stage 4 cancer and live for many years," she says.
"It is scary, because I've never asked my oncologist for any timeline or anything like that, because I don't want to know.
"I think it's just a case of living your life."
What is causing the rise in bowel cancer?
PHS said no definitive cause had been identified for the increase in bowel cancer in people aged under 50 and different potential causes were being investigated.
However, research suggests six in 10 colorectal cancers might be prevented, external through reducing weight, lowering consumption of red and processed meat, increasing dietary fibre and cutting down on alcohol.
Richard Wilson, professor of gastro-intestinal oncology at the University of Glasgow, told BBC Scotland the causes among the under-50s may be different compared with older patients, because of new risk factors that emerged after the 1990s.
"Ultra processed foods, we think, are the huge driver, because their use across all age groups has really increased," he said.
Wilson added that exposure to pesticides as well as micro and nanoplastics might also be factors.
"These tiny broken-down bits of plastic are in the air, in the water, in our food, and we're really concerned about that," he said.
"And then forever chemicals from non-stick frying pans, all of these affect the microbiome in the gut. That's the common denominator.
"We think all these things disrupt the healthy microbiome, cause inflammation, and might predispose to cancer."
Every year thousands of people across Scotland are diagnosed with bowel cancer.
In 2024, 4,275 cases were recorded - slightly down on 2023's figure of 4,395.
NHS inform, external lists the following as potential symptoms of bowel cancer:
- blood in your poo (stools)
- bleeding from your bottom
- a recent change in your poo, particularly looser poo or pooing more regularly
- new pain in your abdomen (tummy) that won't go away
- you've recently lost weight without trying
- more pale and tired than usual
Bowel screening is currently offered to people in Scotland, external aged 50 to 74 years old every two years - this is the same for people in England, external and Wales, external. In Northern Ireland, external screening is offered to people aged 60 to 74 every two years.
A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: "The Scottish government recognises that bowel cancers are occurring at higher rates that previously in people under the age of 50 and have submitted a proposal to the UK National screening committee review bowel screening eligibility to consider offering this to younger age groups."
However, Bowel Cancer UK chief executive Genevieve Edwards said any changes to Scotland's screening programme must be based on "robust evidence" and be supported by the NHS having the capacity to deliver them safely and effectively.
She said the rise in cases among people under 50 showed the need for further research and greater awareness.

01ed085ba6a8f7284ca4e022.title: Bowel cancer cases in under-50s at record high in Scotland
01ed085ba6a8f7284ca4e022.author: Aimee Stanton; Susie Forrest
01ed085ba6a8f7284ca4e022.content:
![Anona Gauld is wearing a pink and black spotty shirt and black glasses. She is smiling and there is a 40th birthday cake in front of her.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/0751/live/be585630-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld had just turned 40 when she was diagnosed with cancer
- Published
The number of people under the age of 50 being diagnosed with bowel cancer in Scotland has reached a record high, with almost 290 new cases in 2024, new figures show.
Bowel cancer is the fourth most common cancer in Scotland and is more often diagnosed in older people, with those over 50 offered screening in an attempt to detect it early.
However, new figures from Public Health Scotland, external show incidence has jumped by 38% in the under-50s over the past decade, with rates among younger women increasing by 56% in comparison with 24% in younger men.
Last month, the Scottish government asked the UK National screening committee to look at lowering the age for bowel screening to 45, to target younger patients.
Anona Gauld is one of a growing number of women under 50 being diagnosed with colorectal cancer, the medical name for bowel cancers.
She told the BBC her journey towards diagnosis started when she turned 40 in March 2023 and couldn't manage a birthday glass of fizz.
She'd had a mysterious pain in her shoulder for several weeks, which got worse every time she drank alcohol.
Gauld, from Stonehaven, thought she'd pulled a muscle or had been lying awkwardly in bed but by August she had been diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer, which had spread to her liver.
![Anona Gauld is wearing a white shirt and black glasses. She has mid length brown hair and is smiling at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/422a/live/d22e2810-9ae3-11f1-b2f7-5d1639b20e22.jpg)
Anona Gauld was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer
She had been going back and forth to her GP over several months but believes cancer wasn't initially considered, partly because of her age.
"One doctor even told me it was because my bra was too tight," she said.
"It was just a mystery."
Doctors later said the pain in her shoulder was actually coming from her liver, where they discovered a 13cm (5in) secondary tumour which had spread from her bowel.
![Lathan is sat in the driver's seat of the car and is smiling at the cancer. Anona is sat next to him.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8857/live/cce81140-9af2-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Anona has three children aged between 15 and 21
"It was a big shock," Gauld says.
"I was young, I was healthy. I had a healthy diet and you don't think it's going to happen to you."
She had chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and then surgery on her liver and bowel in 2024.
Last year the cancer came back in her liver, and since then she's been back on treatment.
"People can have stage 4 cancer and live for many years," she says.
"It is scary, because I've never asked my oncologist for any timeline or anything like that, because I don't want to know.
"I think it's just a case of living your life."
What is causing the rise in bowel cancer?
PHS said no definitive cause had been identified for the increase in bowel cancer in people aged under 50 and different potential causes were being investigated.
However, research suggests six in 10 colorectal cancers might be prevented, external through reducing weight, lowering consumption of red and processed meat, increasing dietary fibre and cutting down on alcohol.
Richard Wilson, professor of gastro-intestinal oncology at the University of Glasgow, told BBC Scotland the causes among the under-50s may be different compared with older patients, because of new risk factors that emerged after the 1990s.
"Ultra processed foods, we think, are the huge driver, because their use across all age groups has really increased," he said.
Wilson added that exposure to pesticides as well as micro and nanoplastics might also be factors.
"These tiny broken-down bits of plastic are in the air, in the water, in our food, and we're really concerned about that," he said.
"And then forever chemicals from non-stick frying pans, all of these affect the microbiome in the gut. That's the common denominator.
"We think all these things disrupt the healthy microbiome, cause inflammation, and might predispose to cancer."
Every year thousands of people across Scotland are diagnosed with bowel cancer.
In 2024, 4,275 cases were recorded - slightly down on 2023's figure of 4,395.
NHS inform, external lists the following as potential symptoms of bowel cancer:
- blood in your poo (stools)
- bleeding from your bottom
- a recent change in your poo, particularly looser poo or pooing more regularly
- new pain in your abdomen (tummy) that won't go away
- you've recently lost weight without trying
- more pale and tired than usual
Bowel screening is currently offered to people in Scotland, external aged 50 to 74 years old every two years - this is the same for people in England, external and Wales, external. In Northern Ireland, external screening is offered to people aged 60 to 74 every two years.
A spokesperson for the Scottish government said: "The Scottish government recognises that bowel cancers are occurring at higher rates that previously in people under the age of 50 and have submitted a proposal to the UK National screening committee review bowel screening eligibility to consider offering this to younger age groups."
However, Bowel Cancer UK chief executive Genevieve Edwards said any changes to Scotland's screening programme must be based on "robust evidence" and be supported by the NHS having the capacity to deliver them safely and effectively.
She said the rise in cases among people under 50 showed the need for further research and greater awareness.
"Scotland's focus must stay on diagnosing bowel cancer earlier and ensuring that everyone receives the right care at the right time," Edwards said.

Bowel remains one of the most common cancer types in Scotland, alongside prostate, breast and lung - these cancers account for more than half (55%) of all diagnoses.

However, there were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, head and neck cancer, bladder cancer, oesophageal cancer and cancer of unknown primary in men.
In women, there were also significant increases in the rates of breast cancer (8%), colorectal cancer (8%), and malignant melanoma of the skin (by more than a third, 37%).
There were no cases of cervical cancer in women under 25 following the introduction of the HPV vaccine.
There were also significant decreases in the rates of lung cancer, cancer of unknown primary, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and kidney cancer.
